text: Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to his father David, at the place David had prepared, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
He began to build on the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign.
These are the foundations Solomon laid for building the house of God: the length, in cubits of the old standard, was sixty cubits, and the width twenty cubits.
The portico in front, running the full width of the house, measured twenty cubits across, and its height was a hundred and twenty cubits; and he overlaid the inside with pure gold.

versions.text: The portico across the front, along the width of the house, was twenty cubits, and its height was a hundred and twenty; and he overlaid the inside with pure gold.
versions.explanation: The measurement "a hundred and twenty" is left without a unit, which is confusing when read aloud; supplying "cubits" matches the preceding measurements. A footnote could also note that some ancient witnesses read twenty cubits for the height.

versions.text: The portico across the front, along the width of the house, was twenty cubits wide, and its height a hundred and twenty cubits; and he overlaid the inside with pure gold.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has a doubled phrase ("in front of the length, in front of the width of the house"), indicating that the portico spanned the whole front breadth of the building. "Twenty cubits wide" can be misread as the portico's depth; "twenty cubits across" makes clear it is the span matching the house's width. The current reading is a defensible rendering but slightly ambiguous when heard aloud.

text: The great hall he paneled with cypress wood, overlaid it with fine gold, and decorated it with palm trees and chains.
He adorned the house with precious stones for beauty, and the gold was gold of Parvaim.
He overlaid the house—its beams, thresholds, walls, and doors—with gold, and he carved cherubim on the walls.
He made the Most Holy Place: its length, corresponding to the width of the house, was twenty cubits, and its width twenty cubits. He overlaid it with six hundred talents of fine gold.
The weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold. He also overlaid the upper rooms with gold.
In the Most Holy Place he made two sculptured cherubim and overlaid them with gold.

The total wingspan of the cherubim was twenty cubits: one wing of the first cherub was five cubits and touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, also five cubits, touched the wing of the other cherub.
Likewise one wing of the second cherub was five cubits and touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, five cubits, met the wing of the first cherub.
The wings of these cherubim spread out twenty cubits. They stood on their feet, facing the main hall.
He made the curtain of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, and worked cherubim into it.
In front of the house he made two pillars, thirty-five cubits high, each with a capital of five cubits on top.
He made chainwork in the inner sanctuary and placed it on top of the pillars; he made a hundred pomegranates and fastened them into the chains.

versions.text: He made chains like those in the inner sanctuary and placed them on top of the pillars; he made a hundred pomegranates and fastened them into the chains.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads simply "he made chains in the inner sanctuary"; "like those in" reflects a conjectural emendation and adds interpretive content not in the text. If the comparative reading is retained, a footnote explaining the difficulty of the Hebrew would be helpful.

text: He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the right and one on the left. The one on the right he named Jachin, and the one on the left Boaz.

versions.text: He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the south and one on the north. The one on the south he named Jachin, and the one on the north Boaz.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says "on the right" and "on the left"; rendering these as south and north is an interpretation based on the temple facing east. Keeping right/left is more faithful, with a footnote noting that since the temple faced east, the right side was to the south.
